item.title: Lawsuit filed challenging Trump’s tariffs on Canada
item.description: A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade. The lawsuit, filed Tuesday by the non-profit Liberty Justice Center on behalf of U.S. food importer Gellert Global Group, argues Trump’s use of a Depression-era trade statute exceeds his power as president. Trump used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap an array of Canadian goods with a 50 per cent levy after trade talks broke down in August. The same statute was used the following month to ban the import of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products. Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht says in a news release that no president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans. The lawsuit asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful and order a refund. More coming Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

item.title: GSMA urges ‘policy reset’ for Canada’s telecom sector
item.description: A new report says the focus of Canada’s telecommunications policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions to invest.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — A new report says the focus of Canada’s telecommunications policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions for companies to invest in their networks at a time when traditional revenues are plateauing and capital costs are expected to rise. The paper from U.K.-based Global System for Mobile Communications Association calls for a “policy reset” that prioritizes affordable and predictable spectrum pricing, support for 5G and AI infrastructure such as data centres, and improved regulatory certainty. It also recommends continued public-private funding to bolster rural and Indigenous connectivity. “Canada is reaching an inflection point in terms of telecoms policy,” said Niall Magennis, senior policy director for the association, which represents more than 1,000 mobile operators and related businesses across the world. “We have to remember that mobile networks play a key role in the economy.” The report said mobile technologies and services generated 5.4 per cent of Canada’s GDP last year, or roughly US$120 billion of economic value — a figure expected to rise to US$170 billion by 2030, thanks to growing adoption of technologies such as 5G, Internet of Things and AI. But Magennis said much of Canada’s telecommunications policy was crafted in the early 2000s. While some elements were appropriate for decades in a high revenue growth environment, especially as elevated immigration levels brought new customers to Canada, the framework has grown outdated in more recent years. The report pointed to Canada’s immigration slowdown, as telecom operators are now attracting fewer new subscribers and seeing their mobile revenues flatten, despite the rising cost of spectrum licences. “Now the sector is experiencing much more of a squeeze,” said Magennis during a presentation Tuesday in Toronto. Carriers are facing other challenges too. While new cellphone plans have become more affordable for consumers — Magennis noted prices have fallen around 25 per cent over the past two years — telecoms are dealing with cost pressures such as the need to fund the next wave of 5G technology, improve network resiliency, and meet obligations around cybersecurity. Magennis said some operators have also waded into AI, building their own data centres and compute facilities at significant costs.  Without a policy shift, he warned that network quality and innovation could gradually weaken. “We need to be mindful that certain policies have effects on investments,” he said. In recent years, the CRTC has introduced various measures aimed at boosting cellphone and internet competition in Canada, empowering consumers, and lowering costs. The regulator has defended those moves while also acknowledging concerns from carriers, some of whom have announced sizable cuts to their capital investment plans in response to the framework. Speaking at an industry conference this past May, CRTC vice-chairperson Adam Scott said the commission is trying to balance multiple priorities, including “affordable prices alongside investment in high-quality networks and broad network coverage.” “I ... see intense competition putting pressure on top-line revenues and making investment cases more challenging. I see population growth slowing and putting further downward pressure on revenue growth,” said Scott at the time. “The balance is the hard part. Overall, I see a better balance than we’ve had in a long time, but those linkages are real.” Magennis, who planned to present his research to the CRTC and Innovation Science and Economic Development Canada this week, said he agrees on the need to find an equilibrium between those competing priorities. “I don’t think it’s one or the other,” he said. “It’s about finding that balance, finding that right level between maybe some shorter-term concerns and then the longer-term view of ‘What does Canada need?’ An element that needs to be factored into that long-term debate is the need to invest in networks, to be ready for not just 5G now, but ... future network technologies.” --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

item.title: Trump drops threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier, citing U.S. jobs
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump has dropped threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier to ban it from the U.S. market and instead vowed to take “good care” of the company’s workers in Kansas.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON/MONTREAL -- U.S. President Donald Trump has dropped threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier to ban it from the U.S. market and instead vowed to take “good care” of the company’s workers in Kansas. Trump’s threats in September against Bombardier became a political issue in Kansas, where it employs 1,500 workers in Wichita. The threatened ban prompted calls to the White House from Kansas lawmakers including Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is facing a tough re-election bid. “We’re going to take care of Bombardier,” Trump told 12 News in Kansas, citing Marshall’s involvement. At a speech Monday, Trump said he would help Bombardier. “I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away... I’ll be helping them because I always viewed them as a Canadian company,” Trump said. “But now I find out they have a presence here, and we’re not hurting them if they’re in Kansas. So we’ll take care of those people and the jobs.” Bombardier’s shares rose four per cent Tuesday after Trump’s comments. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to Trump’s TV interview. Bombardier, which in 1990 acquired Learjet and established its U.S. headquarters in Kansas, has 3,500 jobs in the U.S., more than 40 per cent of which are in Wichita. Bombardier recently announced a North American Learning Center in Kansas and has said it workforce in the state is growing. Last week, it announced a US$50 million investment in Wichita, where it has its defense headquarters, and also plans to open a facility in Fort Wayne, Indiana. Last month, the Trump administration banned a broad swath of Canadian alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and dairy products from import, effective September 29, but took no action against Bombardier. The action came after Canada’s own retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect in early September. Those were prompted after Washington imposed tariffs on some $20 billion of Canadian goods in August, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed. Reuters reported last month it was not immediately clear how Trump could bar Bombardier private jets from being delivered to American customers since they have been approved by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration. Threats by Trump in February to decertify Bombardier aircraft over a certification spat involving U.S. rival Gulfstream Aerospace never materialized, with regulator Transport Canada eventually approving the American-made jets. By David Shepardson and Allison Lampert (Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Jonathan Spicer)

item.content:encoded:
Keith Richards, President, Chief Portfolio Manager, ValueTrend Wealth Management Focus: Technical Analysis

Top Picks: State Street Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR ETF , WSP Global , BMO Equal Weight Global Base Metals Hedged to CAD Index ETF MARKET OUTLOOK: On my last BNN show in September, I called ValueTrend’s approach to the markets as the “buy anything but tech trade”. That, of course, was contrarian in light of the market’s sole focus on tech stocks at the time. It would appear that my call for buying “anything else but tech” is coming to fruition. A rotation into undervalued stocks has begun. My view has not changed. The top 10 stocks now hold roughly 40 per cent of the S&P 500 index. Sheer lunacy!!! Soon, nearly 50 per cent of the S&P will be a roll of the dice on AI.The passive share of the market – aka retail investors- hold Index ETF’s. Their exposure keeps climbing. Moreover, large institutional investors such as pension managers also hold significant passive index exposure. One source I read showed passive index exposure to equities is well over 50 per cent. Why does this matter? More and more equity sits locked down at large institutions and ETF behemoths State Street, Vanguard, and BlackRock, etc. The “market” is becoming dangerously under-diversified and illiquid. These institutions hold the 10 big tech names in They hold & do not sell, given their passive mandate. If & when any of the top tech stocks disappoint – a lack of liquidity will impact them strongly if it becomes a rush to the exits. Why? Well, in a panic selling situation you will have a smaller percentage of buyers, given the huge per cent of float held in passive index platforms. Who will absorb the selling? Hedge funds, individual traders, etc are quick to exit when their sell rules trigger. Look what happened to TXN in June & July – a 30 per cent drop with a massive gap down in one day alone! Decades of trading experience tells me that, in years when the S&P 500 is up on narrow leadership, buying a basket of beaten-down names will dramatically outperform the index from the fourth quarter through the second quarter of the following year. Profit taking, rebalancing overweight positions in the tech names, followed by further pressure on oversold stocks via tax loss selling will likely present massive opportunity in those undervalued names.
